transcript.text: dishwaher leakin water all over the floor and the plug sockets are right next to it whats going on

Water near the plug or socket is dangerous. Please don't touch the plug, socket or machine if they or your hands are wet. If you can do it safely, switch off the circuit at the consumer unit (fuse box), keep away from the water, and don't use the machine again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has checked it. With sockets right next to it, the electrics come first. Leave the dishwasher switched off at the fuse box (consumer unit), don't touch the plug or socket while anything is wet, and don't use the machine again until a qualified engineer or electrician has checked it. Nothing below makes it safe to use. It just helps work out what's leaking. The usual causes of a dishwasher leak, roughly most likely first:
• Foam. Washing-up liquid, or too much dishwasher detergent, makes suds that push out of the door. This is a detergent problem, not a broken part.
• The door seal. A split, flattened or dirty rubber seal, or something caught on it, lets water out at the door edge. Tall items or a damaged spray arm firing water at the door can look exactly the same.
• A hose connection. The inlet hose at the tap, or the drain hose where it joins the sink waste, can work loose or split.
• An internal leak (sump, pump seal or an internal hose). This usually puts water underneath rather than at the door. With the power off at the fuse box and the floor mopped dry, these checks will narrow it down:
1. Look inside. Was there lots of foam in the tub, or could washing-up liquid have gone in (for example, rinse aid or detergent topped up with the wrong bottle)? If so, foam is the most likely culprit and no part is needed.
2. Open the door and run your hand round the rubber seal and along the bottom of the door. Look for splits, flat spots or food caught on it. Damage here points to the seal.
3. Turn each spray arm by hand. Check nothing catches them and no tall trays or utensils hang down in front of the door. Blocking or a cracked arm can spray water straight past the seal.
4. Under the sink, turn the dishwasher's water tap off. Then, without touching any electrics, look at both hose connections for drips, a loose fitting or a split. Wetness here points to the hose rather than the machine. The most useful clue is where the water came from: the front of the door, or from underneath or behind the machine? And was there foam? If the water is coming from underneath with the door and hoses dry, that suggests an internal leak, which is an engineer job anyway.
its still running tho!! water is spreading toward an extension lead on the floor. housemate put fairy washing up liquid in cos we ran out of tablets, theres loads of bubbles at the door. what do i do

Cut the power first, before anything else. 1. Go to the consumer unit (fuse box) and switch off the circuit for the kitchen, or the main switch if you're not sure which one it is. Don't go near the dishwasher, the plug, the socket or the extension lead to do this.
2. If you can't get to the fuse box without walking through water, or the water has already reached the extension lead, get out of the room and call an electrician.
3. Lay towels from the dry side towards the machine to soak up the puddle. Still don't touch the extension lead, plug or sockets. Leave them where they are until they're completely dry and have been checked. As for what's going on, the Fairy is probably the cause. Washing-up liquid makes masses of suds in a dishwasher, far more than it can hold. The foam forces its way out round the door and carries water with it. That's why the bubbles are at the door. It usually means nothing is broken. 1. Leave the door shut for 20–30 minutes so the foam can settle a bit.
2. Open the door with towels on the floor in front. Scoop or sponge out as much foam and water from the bottom of the tub as you can. A jug and a sponge work well.
3. Wipe the door edge and the floor dry. Because water got so close to the extension lead and sockets, please don't switch it back on or run it again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has checked the electrics and the machine. When they're happy it's safe, the usual way to clear leftover suds is an empty rinse with no detergent. If that rinse still puts clear water on the floor with no foam, the door seal or a hose would be the next thing to look at. Going forward, only use dishwasher tablets or powder, never washing-up liquid, even a drop. It would also be worth moving that extension lead permanently off the floor near the dishwasher once it's been checked. Is the power off now?
not yet, im scared to go near it, the water is nearly at the extension lead. fuse box is in the hall so i can get there without going thru the water i think. ill switch it off now

Yes, do that now. 1. Make sure your hands are dry, then flip the main switch (usually the biggest switch, often red, or labelled 'main switch'). That's quicker and surer than hunting for the kitchen circuit. You can sort out which circuit is which later.
2. If you smell burning, see sparks or hear crackling, don't go back into the kitchen. Stay out and call an electrician.
3. Once it's off, the dishwasher will stop and no more water will be pumped out. The water on the floor won't be live any more. Even so, don't touch or move the extension lead or plugs until they're dry and have been checked. As for the cause, the Fairy is probably it. That's why there are bubbles at the door. It's very unlikely anything is broken. Once the power's off, mop up from the dry side and let the foam settle with the door shut. Then you can scoop out the suds as I described. Let me know when it's off and I'll help you with the clean-up.
ok just flipped the main switch, everything in the house went off and the dishwasher stopped. whats next, theres still loads of water

Well done, that was the right call. With the main switch off, nothing in the kitchen is live, so you can deal with the water now. Here's what to do next. 1. Mop up from the dry side inwards. Use towels, a mop and a bucket, wringing them out as you go. Leave the extension lead, plugs and sockets alone. Just soak the water away from around them.
2. Keep the dishwasher door shut for now. Once the floor is mostly dry and the foam has had 20–30 minutes to settle, put a thick towel in front and open it slowly. Then sponge and jug out what's in the bottom of the tub.
3. Wipe the door edge, the front of the machine and the floor dry. If water has gone under the machine, push towels under the front edge as far as you can reach. Don't pull the machine out. On getting the rest of the house back on: once the floor is dry, find the breaker for the kitchen sockets in the consumer unit (it's often labelled 'kitchen' or 'sockets'). If you can't tell which breaker it is, leave the main switch off and get an electrician to help. Your fridge and freezer will be off in the meantime. Keep their doors shut and the food will be fine for a few hours. The cause is probably the Fairy. Washing-up liquid makes far more suds than a dishwasher can contain, and the foam pushes water out round the door. The bubbles at the door fit that exactly, so it's very unlikely anything is broken. Even so, the dishwasher, the extension lead and those sockets mustn't be used again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has checked them, because water got so close. One thing that matters for that check: did the water actually reach the extension lead or any of the sockets, or did it stop short?
it stopped just short i think, the water was nearly at the extension lead but i dont think it got to it. ill start mopping

That's good news. If the water stopped short of the extension lead, the risk is much lower. It still needs checking before anything goes back on, because it's hard to be sure a splash or creeping water didn't reach the lead or the back of a socket. So the dishwasher, that extension lead and those sockets stay unused until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has looked at them. While you mop, a few things will help. 1. Work from the dry side towards the machine, and keep a towel between the puddle and the extension lead as a barrier. Don't touch or move the lead itself.
2. Watch where the water seems to come from. A wet trail from the front of the door, with suds on the door edge, fits the Fairy foam exactly and means nothing is likely broken. Water that keeps appearing from underneath or behind the machine after you've mopped would point more to a hose or an internal leak.
3. When the floor's done, open the door slowly over a towel and scoop out the foam and water from the tub with a jug and sponge. Then glance round the door seal to check it's sitting in place. Heavy foam can occasionally push it out of position. If it all came from the door and there was foam everywhere, the washing-up liquid is probably the whole story. Once the electrics have been checked and given the all-clear, an empty rinse with no detergent will clear the rest of the suds. As you mop, does the water seem to have come from the front of the door, or is some coming from underneath or behind the machine too?
it was the front of the door i think, loads of bubbles there. i didnt see any from underneath

First switch the circuit off at the consumer unit (fuse box); don't touch the plug or socket while anything is wet. That pattern, water coming from the front of the door with loads of bubbles there and nothing from underneath, is exactly what washing-up liquid does in a dishwasher. I'm fairly confident the Fairy is the whole story. The foam is what pushed the water out, so it's very unlikely anything is broken. It still mustn't be switched on or used again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has checked the machine, the extension lead and those sockets, because the water got so close. 1. Then lift out the filter in the base, usually a twist-and-lift cylinder, and rinse it under the tap to get the soapy film off. Less soap left inside means less foam on the first rinse later.
2. Leave the door ajar and towels down overnight so everything dries out, including under the front edge of the machine. One thing makes a real difference to what happens next: which compartment the Fairy went into. If it went in the main detergent drawer, it's a one-off. Once the electrics are cleared, one or two empty rinses with no detergent should clear the rest. If it went into the rinse aid cap, that holds enough for dozens of washes and keeps dosing a little each cycle. It would carry on foaming until that compartment is flushed out, so the engineer would need to know. If it ever leaks clear water with no foam after the suds are gone, that would point to the door seal or a hose instead. Nothing so far suggests that.
ok. the fairy went in the main drawer where the tablet goes i think, not the rinse aid bit. so i just leave it all off till an electrician looks? its my landlords machine

Yes, leave the dishwasher, that extension lead and those sockets off and unused until they've been checked. Because it's your landlord's machine, the next step is theirs to arrange. Landlords are responsible for the appliances and electrics they provide, so let them know today. When you contact them, it helps to tell them plainly:
1. Your housemate used washing-up liquid instead of a dishwasher tablet, and it went in the main detergent drawer, not the rinse aid.
2. The foam pushed water out of the front of the door. None was seen coming from underneath.
3. The water got close to an extension lead and sockets on the floor but seems to have stopped just short. You switched off at the consumer unit as a precaution. Being upfront about the Fairy is worth it. It tells them this is probably a one-off foam problem, not a broken machine. That should mean a quick electrical safety check, then a couple of empty rinses to clear the suds, rather than a repair. Because it went in the main drawer, it won't keep dosing itself the way the rinse aid compartment would. While you wait, these are safe with the power still off:
1. Wipe any leftover Fairy out of the detergent drawer with a damp cloth. Less soap left inside means less foam when it's next run.
2. Keep the door ajar and towels down so it all dries out. Once the floor is dry, you can leave just the kitchen circuit off and get the rest of the house back on, as covered earlier, so your fridge and freezer aren't off for long. If you can't tell which breaker is the kitchen one, leave the main switch off and mention that to the landlord too. After it's been checked and given the all-clear, it only becomes worth looking further if it leaks clear water with no foam. That would point to the door seal or a hose. Nothing so far suggests that.
